articles.title: Japan’s Katayama warns of one-sided yen moves near 160, will coordinate with US Treasury
articles.expand: Katayama’s comments make intervention a more serious risk for anyone pushing dollar-yen above 160, especially as the US has now been confirmed as a willing partner. Expect choppy, headline-driven trading around that level, with dealers alert to any reports of rate checks. The underlying pressure on the yen remains, though, as rising Fed hike expectations keep rate differentials in the dollar’s favour. Oil matters too: higher crude prices raise Japan’s import bill and add to selling pressure on the yen, which is partly why Tokyo is bringing forward energy subsidies. --- Earlier: US Treasury bou...

articles.title: Fed’s Williams says inflation stubbornly high and Fed still has work to do on policy
articles.expand: Williams’ remarks support pricing for a December hike and the dollar’s rate advantage, keeping front-end Treasury yields firm. His emphasis on acting “over time” and on a steady, data-led approach suggests no urgency for a half-point move, which may limit how far bets on a larger hike can build. The comments add to pressure on gold, which has been falling as hike expectations push up real yields. Higher-for-longer messaging also keeps oil-driven inflation risk at the centre of the policy outlook. --- Williams says the Fed has more tightening to do but suggests a steady pace, which supports a D...

articles.title: US Treasury bought yen in July, its first intervention since 1998, as yen nears 160 again
articles.expand: The report confirms that the US is a willing partner in yen support, not just a bystander. That raises the risk for anyone betting heavily on dollar-yen above 160, a level that now looks well defended. Positioning is likely to turn more cautious as the pair approaches the summer’s intervention zone, and volatility could spike on any further rate checks. Rate expectations still favour the dollar, though, because the US economy is resilient and inflation is high. That means intervention may only slow the yen’s slide unless the BOJ follows through with a December hike to 1.5%. --- Yesterday: Japa...

articles.title: UBS sees no RBA cuts until late 2027 as AI boom fuels inflation, growth slowing to 1.4%
articles.expand: UBS’s view is more hawkish than current market pricing, which has moved towards RBA cuts within months. That leaves front-end Australian bond yields exposed if upcoming inflation data run hot. For the Australian dollar, a longer restrictive period would support rate differentials, but the weak domestic growth outlook limits how much it can benefit. The February RBA meeting is now a live risk if quarterly core inflation stays near a 1% pace. UBS’s upbeat global outlook depends partly on a Middle East resolution bringing oil prices down, so a lasting oil shock would hurt both growth and the infl...

Election uncertainty is a near-term drag on business confidence that could weigh on investment decisions until a coalition is formed. With worries of inflation and global rate hikes returning, expectations among investors about an early reopening of the Strait of Hormuz vanished.

articles.title: Trump: I would consider a week-long campaign against Cuba
articles.expand: Trump said he wants to "get Cuba done" before his term ends Would consider "a little bit" of military force Says I will not hesitate to use military force against Iran if necessary It sounds like the plan is to continue blockading Cuba but with Trump you never know, as he improvises nearly everything. Senator Tim Kaine today said he is drafting a provision to end the Iran war that he will demand be attached to a Dec. 11 stopgap spending bill. The 100 level has become a pivot point for the index that measures the U.S. dollar against the other leading reserve currencies. Odds favor continued consolidation, but surprises in the economic or geopolitical landscape could push the dollar index out of its range.

articles.title: Aino Bunge: Interest rates should be adjusted gradually in an uncertain situation
articles.expand: “The Swedish economy is recovering on a broad front, and inflation is expected to rise above target next year. This development justifies a tighter monetary policy, and it is likely that interest rates will be raised further over the coming year. However, any future increases must take into account, not least households’, sensitivity to interest rates." These comments were made by First Deputy Governor Aino Bunge, speaking at Swedbank about the Executive Board’s decision to raise the policy rate to 2 per cent.
